newsitem.title: USA: U.S. said leaning toward backing Zaire force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said leaning toward backing Zaire force.

text.p: The United States is leaning toward backing a proposed protection force for refugees in Zaire but will not itself contribute ground forces, senior officials said on Wednesday.

They also said Washington is providing the United Nations with satellite data so fleeing refugees can be located in Zaire, and faulted Zaire for insisting relief aid be distributed in Rwanda and Burundi instead of Zaire, where 1.2 million refugees are said to be at risk.

"That's a very strong inclination here," one senior official said when asked if Washington might support such a military protection force, which has been under discussion in recent days as the crisis in Zaire worsened.
Officials stressed, however, that no formal decision has been made, despite what Washington acknowledges is an emergency situation, and many details need to be resolved.
They emphasized that if such a force were created, the United States would only provide logistical support, not ground troops.

After the 1994 Rwanda killings which left more than 500,000 people dead, mostly minority Tutsis, a million Hutus fled to eastern Zaire, including soldiers and militia. The crisis escalated recently when ethnic Tutsis in Zaire fought the Zairean army, with the refugees caught in the crossfire.

An eight-nation African summit in Nairobi on Tuesday called for the United Nations to send a "neutral" protection force to create havens or corridors from which the mostly ethnic Hutu refugees could go home along safe corridors.
France, pushing the hardest for intervention, is said to want the force to be 5,000-strong and multinational.

France and Spain have pledged around 1,000 troops, but Rwanda considers Paris pro-Hutu and is believed to want France to stay away. The United States, African and other nations have seemed lukewarm to the idea.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters Washington is reviewing all proposals put forward.

"Some of the proposals would require logistical support by the United States Armed Forces. We're not talking about ground force units here (but) logistical support. And we're looking at that question," he said.
Another senior official said there was "healthy skepticism" in the administration about the proposed use of a multinational force.

But Washington would be hard-pressed not to back the force as it has been pushing over the past month for creation of an all-Africa crisis response force which could act in similar crises in the future.
Officials said the proposals were changing daily, creating confusion. Questions about what is a safe corridor and what troops might be involved have not been answered, they said.

"We want to work internationally with our partners to try to help in Eastern Zaire. But we've got to be assured that the plans are sound, that they're logical and that they would work," Burns told a news briefing.
Efforts to help refugees stranded in the war zone of eastern Zaire reached a stalemate on Wednesday, with Zaire telling aid agencies to keep out and the United Nations saying many lives were at risk.

"We are asking humanitarian organizations to stop distributing any aid to the refugees on Zairean soil. They must instead distribute aid in Rwanda and Burundi," said Zairean spokesman Boguo Makeli, whose government wants the refugees out.
Aid dried up last week when aid workers fled fighting. The United Nations refugee agency UNHCR says many lives will be lost unless they take food and medicine back into Zaire fast.
